description: Features of the gurdwara, langar, Nam Japna and Sikh daily prayer.
content_html:
The Gurdwara

The gurdwara (‘Gate of the Guru’) is the Sikh place of worship and community. The Rahit Maryada (Sikh code of conduct), Chapters 4–6, provides detailed guidance on the proper use and conduct of the gurdwara. At the centre of every gurdwara is the Guru Granth Sahib — treated as a living presence rather than merely a book.

Key features of the gurdwara: the takht (the raised throne on which the Guru Granth Sahib rests); the chanani (canopy over the Guru Granth Sahib); the chaur (fan waved over the Guru Granth Sahib as a sign of reverence); the Nishan Sahib (the Sikh flag flown outside, marking the gurdwara’s presence to the community); and the langar hall.

Key Fact

The four doors of the gurdwara (doors on all four sides) signify that the gurdwara is open to all people — from all four directions, all castes, all genders, all religions. This is the architectural embodiment of the Sikh teaching on equality. Guru Granth Sahib page 1391 affirms that the gurdwara belongs to all — it is the Guru’s house, open to everyone.

The Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple)

The most sacred gurdwara in the world is the Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple) in Amritsar, Punjab. Founded by Guru Arjan Dev (the fifth Guru) in the late 16th century, it is surrounded by a sacred pool (the Amrit Sarovar, ‘Pool of Nectar’). The Harmandir Sahib has four doors on all four sides — the architectural statement that it is open to all humanity. The Guru Granth Sahib is present inside day and night, and scripture is read continuously. It is both a pilgrimage site and a living gurdwara.

Langar

Langar is the communal kitchen and free meal served in every gurdwara to all who visit, regardless of their faith, caste, gender or background. Guru Granth Sahib page 967 teaches that serving and sharing with others is a form of devotion. The langar was instituted by the Sikh Gurus as a direct rejection of the caste system: by eating together at the same level (sitting on the floor), all social distinctions are dissolved before God.

The langar is also an expression of sewa (selfless service) — the volunteers who cook, serve and clean in the langar are performing tan sewa (physical service). In large gurdwaras, including the Harmandir Sahib, tens of thousands of meals are served daily, making it one of the largest acts of communal feeding in the world.

The spec requires awareness of divergences between Khalsa and non-Khalsa Sikhs. Both are welcome in the gurdwara and at the langar; the gurdwara is open to all. Khalsa Sikhs — those who have undergone Amrit Sanskar — bear the Five Ks and follow the full Rahit Maryada. Non-Khalsa Sikhs follow the same core teachings but have not taken formal initiation. In practice, in most gurdwaras, the reader of the Guru Granth Sahib (the granthi) will typically be Khalsa. The langar and sangat are equally open to all.

Nam Japna: Meditating on God’s Name

Nam Japna (‘repeating the Name’) is the practice of meditating on and repeating the name of God — usually ‘Waheguru’ (‘Wonderful Lord’). Guru Granth Sahib page 1142 teaches that Nam Japna transforms the practitioner: through the repetition of God’s name, the mind becomes purified, haumai (ego) is gradually dissolved, and the soul moves toward mukti (liberation).

Nam Japna takes several forms: silent personal meditation; recitation during daily prayers; and communal singing of hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib (kirtan). It is practised at home, in the gurdwara, and through engagement with the Nitnem (daily prayers).

Sikh Daily Prayer

Sikh daily life is structured around prayer. Guru Granth Sahib page 305 teaches the importance of prayer both in the morning and at night, reminding Sikhs to orient every day around the divine. The Nitnem consists of five set prayers: Japji Sahib (morning), Jaap Sahib and Tav-Prasad Savaiye (morning), Sodar Rahiras Sahib (evening) and Kirtan Sohila (bedtime). These prayers come from the Guru Granth Sahib and are the daily framework for a gurmukh (God-centred) life.

Key Fact

Nam Japna (GGS 1142) is the daily meditation on God’s name, typically ‘Waheguru’ (Wonderful Lord). It dissolves haumai (ego) and moves the soul toward mukti. The 2.5* comparison point asks for contrast with Christian prayer — note that Nam Japna is primarily meditative repetition of God’s name, while Christian prayer (Lord’s Prayer, Matthew 6:9–13) is primarily address to a personal God in words of praise, petition and confession.
exam_tip_html: For the 5-mark question, your named sources are: Guru Granth Sahib 1391 (gurdwara open to all), Guru Granth Sahib 967 (langar as service and devotion), Guru Granth Sahib 1142 (Nam Japna transforms the mind) and Guru Granth Sahib 305 (daily prayer). The 2.5* comparison-marked spec point on prayer requires you to contrast Sikh prayer (Nam Japna, Nitnem) with Christian prayer (Lord’s Prayer, Matthew 6:9–13) — develop both sides. The most common error is describing the Guru Granth Sahib as merely ‘a holy book’ — in Sikhism it is treated as the living eternal Guru, not an inert text. SPaG rewards correct spelling of ‘Harmandir Sahib’, ‘Nishan Sahib’, ‘chanani’ and ‘Nam Japna’.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The gurdwara features: Guru Granth Sahib on the takht, chanani and chaur (marks of reverence), Nishan Sahib outside, langar hall, and four doors (symbolising openness to all). Guru Granth Sahib 1391 affirms its universal welcome. The Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar is the most sacred gurdwara.
  • Langar (GGS 967) is the free communal meal served to all visitors as an expression of sewa and the equality of all before God. It is both a practical act of service and a daily embodiment of Sikh equality teaching.
  • Nam Japna (GGS 1142) is meditating on God’s name (‘Waheguru’) to dissolve haumai and move toward mukti. Daily prayers (GGS 305) structure the gurmukh Sikh’s day around the divine. This is the 2.5* comparison spec point with Christian prayer.

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of a gurdwara and their significance.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three features with brief significance. Acceptable: takht (raised throne on which the Guru Granth Sahib rests, showing its status as eternal Guru); chanani (canopy over the GGS, a mark of royal honour and respect); chaur (fan waved over the GGS, sign of reverence); Nishan Sahib (orange/blue flag outside, marks the gurdwara's presence); four doors (open on all sides to all people, embodying Sikh equality); langar hall (communal kitchen serving free food to all).

practice_questions.text: Describe the langar and why it is important for Sikhs today.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks. Langar is the free communal meal served in every gurdwara to all visitors regardless of background (1 mark). It expresses sewa (selfless service) — GGS 967 teaches that sharing with others is devotion (1 mark). It embodies Sikh equality: all sit on the floor at the same level, dissolving caste and social distinctions in the Guru's presence (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Nam Japna is important for Sikh religious life.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per way. Way 1: Nam Japna (GGS 1142) dissolves haumai (ego) — through repeated meditation on God's name the mind becomes purified and the soul moves toward mukti; it is the practical means by which a gurmukh Sikh overcomes the self-centredness of the manmukh. Way 2: Nam Japna is practised both individually (silent meditation, personal prayer) and communally (kirtan — singing hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib), binding the Sikh community in shared devotion and structuring both the individual's day and the congregation's worship.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two differences between Sikh and Christian worship.
In your answer, include a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 + 2 marks + 1 for named source. Difference 1: Sikh prayer (Nam Japna) is primarily meditative repetition of God's name ('Waheguru') to purify the mind and dissolve ego; Christian prayer (Lord's Prayer) is primarily addressed to a personal God in words of praise, petition and confession. Difference 2: Sikh worship centres on the Guru Granth Sahib as the living eternal Guru; Christian worship in the Mass (Catholic) or liturgical service centres on the Bible reading and, for Catholics, the Eucharist as Christ's real presence. 5th mark: ‘Guru Granth Sahib 305 teaches the importance of prayer morning and night, structuring the Sikh day around the divine’ or cite Matthew 6:9-13 for the Lord's Prayer.

practice_questions.text:
'The gurdwara is the most important institution in Sikh religious life.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion. Arguments in support: the gurdwara is where the Guru Granth Sahib (eternal Guru) is present and treated as a living reality; all major Sikh ceremonies (Amrit Sanskar, Naam Karan, Akhand Path) take place there; the langar (GGS 967) makes equality visible and feeds the community; the four doors embody Sikh teaching on equality; Guru Granth Sahib 1391 affirms it as open to all. Arguments against: the Guru Granth Sahib itself, not the building, is the eternal Guru — Sikh worship and Nam Japna can take place at home; the sangat can meet wherever Sikhs gather; the three core duties (Nam Japna, kirat karni, vand chakna) can be practised without a gurdwara; for Sikhs living as a minority without a nearby gurdwara, home devotion and the Nitnem maintain the gurmukh life. Secure (7-9): Both sides; at least GGS 1391 or GGS 967 named. Developing (4-6): One-sided. Emerging (1-3): Brief.

practice_questions.text: Outline three reasons why the Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple) is important to Sikhs worldwide.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each. Acceptable: it is the most sacred gurdwara in Sikhism, a global centre of pilgrimage and spiritual significance; it was founded by Guru Arjan Dev and the Guru Granth Sahib is present continuously; the four doors embody Sikh equality (open to all); it is surrounded by the sacred pool (Amrit Sarovar); tens of thousands of langar meals are served daily; it is the architectural and spiritual heart of Sikhism.

knowledge_checks.q: What do the four doors of the gurdwara symbolise?
options: The four seasons of worship throughout the year
The four stages of Sikh initiation
The openness of Sikhism to all people from all directions
The four Sikh Gurus who built the gurdwara

glossary_terms.definition: The Sikh place of worship; literally 'Door (or Gate) of the Guru', the central institution of Sikh community life.
The raised platform or throne on which the Guru Granth Sahib is placed; the focal point of every gurdwara.
The embroidered canopy suspended above the Guru Granth Sahib as a mark of respect and royal honour.
The whisk or fan waved over the Guru Granth Sahib as a sign of reverence; an ancient symbol of royal honour.
The orange or dark-blue triangular Sikh flag flown outside every gurdwara, indicating its presence to the community.
The communal kitchen in the gurdwara where free food is prepared and served to all visitors regardless of background.
The 'Temple of God', also known as the Golden Temple; the most sacred gurdwara in Sikhism, located in Amritsar.
The holy city of Sikhism in Punjab, India; location of the Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple).
The communal kitchen and free meal served in every gurdwara to all visitors, as an expression of sewa and equality.
Meditating on and repeating the name of God; one of the three core Sikh duties, practised through silent meditation and communal kirtan.
